name: Pedro Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me what a normal working day is like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Pedro, 43, and I operate a bolting rig at the large mine. I check the roof map, set the rig, drill and seat anchors, then record the torque before the next crew comes through; I like seeing a section made safe. The part that wears me down is waiting for a new map while a panel is closed. My partner Nadia drives a delivery van, and we have two children in school and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the bolting crew a tidier report is useful if it puts the right roof readings in front of the next shift. I have asked an AI tool for a plain explanation of a machine warning before, but I still checked the service book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rig work stays mine in this picture, and my partner Nadia's delivery-van route keeps paying too. We have nearly five months of expenses saved, so the mortgage feels steady even when one of us misses a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep operating the bolting rig and mark each anchor on the roof map after the shift. If a new report form arrives in the first year, I'd compare it with the service book and ask the safety officer to correct any missing reading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly relaxed about a small paperwork change. I would still rather see a smudged true number than a neat invented one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which reading matters most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The torque reading tells us whether the bolt is seated properly. I once found a row copied from the previous panel, so I went back and measured before signing the map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Nadia say about the van route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Nadia says parcels still have to reach actual doors. A quicker route sheet might give her an earlier finish, which would be welcome with our two children in school.

say: I would welcome **tidier roof reports** if readings stay accurate.
I would **check AI explanations** against the service book.
think: I expect **both current wages** to hold in this picture.
Our **five-month reserve** steadies the mortgage through a missed shift.
do: Keep operating the **bolting rig** and marking roof anchors on every shift.
Compare new **report forms** with the service book.
feel: **Relaxed** about paperwork, careful about invented numbers.
S0.quote: I would still rather see a smudged true number than a neat invented one.
fieldNote: Pedro checks **torque readings** himself after seeing a copied row in the roof map.
Both **paid routes** look secure under small change, and household savings cover nearly five months.

steps.text: Keep paid bolting-rig shifts and mark roof anchors after work
Compare any new report form with service book readings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say mine engineers may get faster plans and parcel firms may use better booking before robots reach our hands-on jobs. I would ask our supervisor to test any roof-map software beside a bolter, not alone at a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A quicker plan could cut the pauses between panels, and those pauses are sometimes paid overtime for me. Nadia's van routes might be packed tighter too, so both of us could lose a little income without losing a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join a roof-map trial after two experienced operators have used it, then record where it misses a cracked seam. If overtime falls in the first year, Nadia and I would pause the new kitchen cupboards and put the difference in our monthly bills account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel willing to try a proven tool, but careful about the pay slips. A faster map should not quietly erase the time it takes to make the roof safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test a cracked seam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the software's bolt pattern with the chalk marks from our physical check. If the pattern skips the weak strip, we stop and ask engineering before drilling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Nadia do if routes tighten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She would compare the paid delivery hours with the parcel count for a month. Nadia knows a short route on the screen can still mean a long queue at apartment doors.

say: I would test **roof-map software** beside experienced bolters.
I would say **engineering plans** change before hands-on rig work.
think: I worry **overtime** may fall as plans become faster.
I worry Nadia’s **van income** may also shrink through tighter routes.
do: Join a **roof-map trial** after two operators test it.
feel: **Willing to try** a proven tool, wary about wages.
S1.quote: A faster map should not quietly erase the time it takes to make the roof safe.
fieldNote: Pedro’s openness is **conditional on operator testing** against chalk marks on the rock.
His pay concern is **overtime erosion**, alongside tighter delivery routes for Nadia.

steps.text: Trial roof-map software after two experienced operators test it
Keep paid bolting shifts and log cracked seams software misses
Pause kitchen cupboards if overtime falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI by 2028 could change engineering plans and parcel booking, with capable bolting and delivery robots around 2031. I would ask both employers to say what jobs remain before they order machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The roof still needs a rig operator after thinking AI arrives, but I expect many bolting shifts to go when robots can install anchors. Nadia could lose her van route around the same time, and five months saved cannot cover two missing wages for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine training manager this month which ground-control inspection jobs need a certificate, and Nadia would ask the depot for its fleet plans. In 2029 I'd keep bolting while applying for a posted mine ground-inspection assistant job, and we'd make a mortgage-only budget if either employer issued notices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would lie awake over the possibility of both wages ending close together. Knowing how to use a tool on my phone would not make us safe from a machine that can do the whole rig job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take the inspection job at lower pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would calculate the actual wage and travel cost before saying yes. Some nearby mines have ground crews, but a vacancy and a fair wage are different things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our children that we might have to spend less for a while, but their school and friends are not changing on a rumour. Nadia and I would only discuss a move after one of us had a written offer.

say: I would distinguish **2028 planning AI** from bolting robots around 2031.
I would seek **remaining-job plans** from both employers.
think: I expect many **bolting shifts** to disappear with robots.
I fear Nadia’s **van route** could end at the same time.
do: Apply for a **posted inspection assistant job** nearby.
feel: **Sleepless worry** about losing both household wages.
S2.quote: Knowing how to use a tool on my phone would not make us safe from a machine that can do the whole rig job.
fieldNote: Pedro separates **2028 thinking tasks** from the 2031 threat to bolting and delivery routes.
He would check **wages and travel costs** before treating nearby inspection work as an answer.

steps.text: Keep paid bolting-rig shifts through 2029 and ask about inspection certificates
Apply for posted ground-inspection assistant role at nearby mine
Make mortgage-only budget if either employer issues a job notice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI in 2031 and capable rig robots around 2034 give us several years to train on safe ground checks. I would want the mine to publish a paid path from bolting into inspection rather than guessing who can transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I could still run the rig while engineers use AI, and at 51 I may need other paid work. I could learn inspection work with time, but I cannot assume Nadia's depot or my mine will keep everyone on wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine's senior inspector this winter to let me observe a ground survey once a month. If the college's inspection certificate has an evening place we can afford, I'd enrol; in 2032 I'd keep bolting and apply for a paid inspection trainee post if advertised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to make a measured choice. I am still anxious that a new certificate could arrive in a market with fewer jobs than applicants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn on a ground survey?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How inspectors record a crack before it reaches the roof line, and which reading means the panel must close. My rig experience helps me notice things, but I would need supervised hours to sign a survey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could use a small piece of the savings if the fee is modest and both wages continue. I would not drain the reserve, because a van repair or an unpaid shift can still happen.

say: I would seek a **paid inspection path** before 2034 rig robots.
I would use the years before **2031 AI** to learn safe ground checks.
think: I may need **different wages** by age 51.
I cannot assume either employer will **retain everyone** through automation.
do: Observe a **monthly ground survey** if allowed.
Enrol in an **affordable evening certificate** if offered.
Apply for a **paid trainee post** in 2032 if advertised.
feel: **Able to choose**, anxious about scarce inspection jobs.
S3.quote: My rig experience helps me notice things, but I would need supervised hours to sign a survey.
fieldNote: Pedro is prepared to spend a **small part of savings** on a certificate while protecting the reserve.
He knows his **rig experience** does not replace supervised inspection hours.

steps.text: Keep paid bolting shifts and observe monthly ground surveys if permitted
Enrol in evening inspection certificate if affordable and offered
Apply for paid inspection trainee post in 2032 if advertised

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew ten years to thinking AI and bolting robots around 2039 is enough time to demand an honest mine plan. The people who know the roof should help decide what a robot must prove before a panel reopens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when full thinking AI arrives and 56 when robots can install bolts. Our children will be adults then, but the mortgage may remain, and I do not know what our pensions will actually pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep bolting and request both pension statements this year so Nadia and I can see the figures. We'd add a fixed payment to mortgage principal while our routes remain paid; in 2037 I'd compare actual inspection openings with my wage and qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady about the next few years and glad there is time to decide. I would be uneasy if the mine used the distant date as a reason to avoid telling us its machine plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire when the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the after-tax pension income and mortgage balance make sense together. I do not know our after-tax pension income or mortgage balance yet, so I would not promise retirement at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an inspection job worth leaving the rig?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real offer with a wage close enough to cover our bills and hours I can manage. The children should be grown, but I would still want time to see Nadia after her route ends.

say: I would demand an **honest mine plan** before 2039 bolting robots.
I would include **roof operators** in proving robot safety.
think: I may still need **paid work** at 56 despite grown children.
I cannot assume **pensions** cover a remaining mortgage.
do: Keep **paid bolting shifts** and request pension figures.
Pay extra **mortgage principal** while both routes pay.
feel: **Steady soon**, uneasy about delayed mine plans.
S4.quote: I do not know our after-tax pension income or mortgage balance yet, so I would not promise retirement at 56.
fieldNote: Pedro considers **after-tax pension income** and mortgage balance rather than assuming retirement at 56.
His 2037 check uses **real inspection offers** and qualifications, while he continues paid rig work.

steps.text: Keep paid bolting-rig shifts and request household pension statements
Add fixed mortgage-principal payment while both household routes pay
Compare posted inspection openings and wages with rig work in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because both the bolting rig and Nadia's van route could face capable robots around 2031. A fleet plan, paid inspection training and real trainee openings would help us prepare. I can learn carefully, but two wages cannot be replaced with a brochure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who signs the roof map when a robot seats the anchors. I want a named inspector to check torque and carry responsibility before another crew enters.

headlineQuote: I can learn carefully, but two wages cannot be replaced with a brochure.
portrait: Pedro is a **43-year-old bolting-rig operator** with two school-age children, a mortgage and nearly five months saved.
He sometimes uses **AI tools**, but verifies machine warnings and roof readings in service records.
He expects **engineering AI** before robots threaten his rig and Nadia’s delivery route.
He would pursue **ground-inspection training** while preserving paid shifts and household savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may bring bolting and delivery robots around 2031, threatening both household wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **fleet plan**, paid inspection training and real trainee openings would help Pedro prepare.
